speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I desire to read an Ottawa dispatch which appeared in the Toronto * World ' of Friday morning last. The dispatch is as follows:
Ottawa, April 27 (Special).-The sensatioaal charges made by a Toronto newspaper against one of the ministers of the federal government Mr. FISHER.
at Ottawa was no surprise here. The facts of the case have been pretty well known for some time and it is expected that the matter will come up in parliament at an early date.
It is understood that Hon. Frank Oliver Is the minister against whom the charge is made. The story at Ottawa is that Mr. Oliver had an order in council passed on May 8, 1907, giving the Canadian Northern railway the power to select in Saskatchewan the whole of the land granted by the government to the Manitoba and Southeastern, which is the Canadian Northern in Manitoba, in 1890, in all 600,000 acres. In 1907, there were no lands left in Manitoba, it was alleged, and the company was given the right to select its lands in Saskatchewan.	,
In the same year, $50,000 was deposited from the Manhattan Bank of New York to the Imperial Bank at Edmonton in the name of Mr. Oliver. The exact date was October 3, 1907. About one year later, just before the general election of 1908, the sum of $19,000 was deposited from the Manhattan Bank in the name of Mr. Oliver at the Imperial Bank at Edmonton. It is known that he chequed out this money for campaign purposes.
It will be observed that without making a direct statement the dispatch- gives currency to two separate rumours or reports, one relating to a transaction affecting the land grant of the Manitoba Southeastern Railway Company, and the other relating to an account kept in my name in the Imperial Bank of Edmonton. No connection between the land transaction and the bank account is alleged or inferred in words, but there can be no doubt that the two paragraphs have been placed together for the purpose of creating an impression in the public mind that there is some connection -and an improper connection-between them.
So that there may be no misunderstanding of my position I desire to state without qualification that there is no foundation for such an insinuation. In regard to the land transaction mentioned, I desire to say that the action taken by the government was on my recommendation, and that I made the recommendation in pursuance of what I believed to be sound public policy and with due regard to the public interest, and that I received no money, or other consideration for having made that recommendation, or in any way in connection with it. Although no specific charge has been made, I desire that the fullest opportunity shall be given to lay such a charge. I would, therefore, respectfully ask that a special committee may be appointed to hear and inquire into any charge that may be made in connection with the transaction mentioned.

Before going on with the orders of the day, I would like to ask the First Minister the name of the man who made the charge to him that has been

referred to by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) just now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Well, I accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I have a question which I would like to ask. Acting on the precedent of the Hodgins charges, does the First Minister propose any investigation in this matter?

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to draw your attention again very briefly to the Farmers' Bank. In view of the previous discussion this session it will not be necessary for me to go very deeply into the matter, and I can confine myself to the records contained in certain returns that have been brought down to the House. The Farmers' Bank was incorporated in>
1904. I have nothing at all to say in reference to the incorporation of the bank originally. The Bank Act gives them a year in which to organize and get subscriptions, and as they failed to do that within the year they came back to parliament in 1905 and the Banking and Commerce Committee thought well to renew their charter for another year. They came back again in the spring of 1906 and again asked for an extension for another year and they were granted an extension of six months. I recognize that the Minister of Finance has a duty common to all members of the committee to scrutinize the legislation proposed, and I have no doubt he discharged that duty then. It 259
may be that the Minister of Finance, by reason, of his position has a greater obligation on him than an ordinary member of the committee, but I am not disposed to urge that view at present more than to say that, having regard to the failure of these people during two years to put themselves in a financial Position to transact business, the minister tells us he was reluctant to grant them an extension of time. That was significant only in that the mind of the Finance Minister being set in that direction at that time, we would apprehend that he would remain seized of that idea and that he would exercise even greater diligence and care, in scrutinizing the application of the bank for a certificate to do business. Further than that I have nothing to say at all with reference to the propriety or impropriety of incorporating this company. I am not aware that the Minister of Finance mentioned to the House when the Bill came before it finally the difficulties he felt in regard to the extension of time. I would- suppose that probably the minister, feeling that it was doubtful whether this company should be granted an extension of time, might have felt it incumbent on him to mention to the House the doubt in his mind. However, I will let that point go. 1 come, therefore, to deal with the question of granting the certificate and the first point I have to refer to in that connection is the letter of Mr. Leighton McCarthy, which was mailed to the minister on the 8th of October,! 1906, frt>m Toronto. I need not read that letter further than to say' that Mr. McCarthy assures the minister. that grave conditions have arisen requiring careful consideration by the Treasury Board before granting a certificate, and Mr. McCarthy asks that an opportunity be afforded him of discussing the matter with the minister and he mentions that he could come down to Ottawa at any time if the circumstances are urgent, but he would prefer not to come until the following week. That letter was not answered spontaneously, and it was followed on the 11th of October by a telegram from Mr. McCarthy, and that telegram was answered on the same date by the Finance Department. But the letter of the 11th of October to Mr. McCarthy from the department ignores his suggestion that he should be given a personal interview. It intimates that a personal interview is not desired and simply tells Mr. McCarthy to forward his representations and they will receive due consideration. In other words, so far as I can see, the Minister of Finance, to use the phrase of the Prime Minister, was not actuated by any great feeling of curiosity at that time.



We come then to the letter of the 19th October from Mr. McCarthy, an important letter. It says:
I beg to inclose the special endorsement upon a writ of summons in the High Court of Justice of Ontario, which will be issued by Wm. A Dixon and others. The names of about a dozen persons are given as plaintiffs.
This letter was sent to the hon. Minister of Finance in pursuance of what Mr. McCarthy said he wanted to do, namely, to call the attention of the department to certain irregularities and frauds in connection with the obtaining of stock subscriptions for the Farmers' Bank. In that letter Mr. McCarthy points out that this suit is not merely on behalf of those named, but also of other subscribers to shares who come in and join in it. He also goes on to say that not only the grounds alleged in the special endorsement, but other grounds which may be disclosed upon the examination of the alleged subscribers for shares will be furnished. Mr. McCarthy then proceeds to say:
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name^ of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or a sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
Mr. McCarthy concludes by saying:
I would be pleased to go to Ottawa upon any appointment you may make for the further consideration of this matter.
This was the second offer from Mr. McCarthy to go to Ottawa and have a personal interview with the minister and disclose to him all the facts and circumstances which prompted Mr. McCarthy to say that the whole business had been initiated in fraud.
It is necessary that we should refer to some of the statements contained in the special endorsement upon the writ which Mr. McCarthy forwarded to the Minister of Finance. This special endorsement says:
That the subscriptions for shares which were procured from the plaintiffs and others were procured through fraud and misrepresentation.
I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that this endorsement is not confined to eight or ten, or a dozen names of parties who allege fraud, but it goes on to say that Dr. Stewart was represented as subscribing for shares to the amount of $10,000, whereas in fact he had not subscribed for any shares. That Major Beattie, represented by the inspectors to have consented to act as a director, had not sub-Mr. LENNOX.
scribed for any shares, and refused to be a director, and refused to allow his name to be used in anv way in connection with the bank; and that names of others were represented by the inspectors to have consented to act as directors who had not subscribed for any shares, or given any authority for any such publication. Then it goes on to say:
And the plaintiffs allege that the acts and proceedings of the provisional directors were illegal and irregular; that the agents and sol-licitors, professing to act under the name and authority of the provisional directors procured a large number of subscribers for shares, and received the sum of about $175,000 more or less on account thereof, and also procured promissory notes to be signed by persons who were subscribing for shares, and these persons were endeavouring to discount these notes for the purpose of meeting the $250,000 that had to be deposited with the government.
Then it goes on:
That persons professing to act under the authority of the provisional directors did unlawfully deduct large sums for alleged services and commissions and other purposes out of the moneys received by them.
And the plaintiffs further allege:
That the shares and the money and the promissory notes procured from them were procured through fraud, deceit and misrepresentation ; and that all money, promissory notes and other obligations received as aforesaid by all persons acting or professing to act in the name of and on behalf of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, or of the provisional directors, or any of them, are impressed with a trust in favour of all the subscribers for shares who may desire to come in and become parties to the action.
I read this special endorsement for the purpose of calling the attention of the Minister of Finance to this point, that whilst there were specific allegations with reference to twelve or thirteen who were beginning the proceedings, there were general allegations of fraud, misconduct, irregularities and disregard of the Bank Act as to the transactions generally of the Farmers' Bank and its representatives in obtaining the right to transact business.
It will be noted that Mr. McCarthy asks for an interview, and that his letter of the 19th October was not answered until the 23rd. And it is a significant fact that all through this correspondence, every letter that affected the Farmers' Bank, or Mr. Travers, was acted upon, and answered with an amazing degree of promptitude, whereas everything that interested the public was delayed or ignored.
Eeplying to this letter to Mr. McCarthy, of the 23rd October, 1906, the deputy minister said:
I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th inst. to Mr. Fielding's ad-

dress respecting the Farmers' Bank of Canada. When application is made by the Farmers' Bank to the Treasury Board for a .certificate to enable them to commence business, the representations contained in your letter with its. inclosure will be laid before the Board.
That was never done.
Hear, hear.

I noticed during the last discussion that it was alleged that probably that was not done. Well, I have here the means of proving absolutely that it was never done. You will note that Mr. McCarthy urged at least twice that he be granted an interview so that he might discuss the whole matter with the minister. As a member of parliament he had a duty to discharge, and he desired to have the minister seized of the whole situation both as regards his clients and the public generally, and the other subscribers to the shares. But for some reason the minister absolutely ignored the petition of one of his own supporters to have this matter investigated in the satisfactory way in which it might have been investigated, if this interview had been consented to. On October 23, Mr. Travers forwards the receipt for that $250,000 deposit, and on October 24, with that promptness which has characterized this branch of the case, the very day upon which it was received, the deputy minister writes acknowledging the receipt of the money and says:
I may say in this connection that opposition has been filed_ in this department to the granting of a certificate to your bank under section 11 of the Bank Act.

For Deputy Minister of Finance.
On October 29, we have this amazing letter from Mr. Travers:
„	Toronto, October 29, 1906.
The Hon,
The Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-Yours of the 24th, post-marked October 26, was received here on the 27th.
I was surprised to know that any one had filed an opposition against this bank being granted a certificate.
Would you kindly do me the favour of supplying me with a copy of the said objections, as I do not know up to the present moment wherein we have deviated in the slightest effect from the Bank Act.

General Manager.
At that time, on October 29, when Mr. Travers wrote this letter and on October 30, when it was received in the Department of Finance, the department by perusal of the newspapers to which allusion has been made, possessed full and ample knowledge that that statement was absolutely false, and it is not unimportant that we should 2591
keep that point firmly in mind. The Finance Minister knew at that time, as I submit, that the statement of Mr. Travers that he was not aware of any irregularity or any charge that could possibly be made against him was not in accordance with the facts.
On October 30, 1906, a letter was addressed to Mr. Leighton G. McCarthy, as follows:
Ottawa, Oct. 31, 1906. Leighton G. McCarthy, Esq., K.C., M.P., Toronto, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 19th instant, addressed to Mr. Fielding, on the subject of the Farmers' Bank of Canada and the issue of a certificate to that bank to commence business under section 15 of the Bank Act, I notice recently a reference in the newspapers for a judgment given by Judge Anglin in a suit relating to this matter. In view of the decision rendered, I shall be obliged if you will let me know if you still desire the protest contained in your letter to be brought before the Treasury Board upon an application of the Farmers' Bank for a certificate to be considered.

For Deputy Minister of Finance.
That I venture to say is a somewhat remarkable letter. Why did the Deputy Minister write that letter at all? He says he has noticed something in the newspapers, and he, therefore, thinks it is right to ask Mr. McCarthy to withdraw the protest he had entered, and which Mr. McCarthy wanted to supplement by a viva voce interview with the minister. It is worth while to ascertain just what the position was in regard to the newspaper matter. Was the newspaper account one that would allay suspicion, and that would lead the Department of Finance to think that all was right or was it one to add to their suspicion, and give them additional reasons for not granting a certificate? I have taken pains to look into that question, and I find that the case came up in court on Saturday October 27, and the account of it appeared in the Toronto papers, on Monday, October 29. It would reach Ottawa on the evening of Monday, October 29. Again I call attention to the promptness with which the Department of Finance deals with anything that will help Travers to get through this charter. On October 29, items appeared in the Toronto papers. They are 'sensational items, covering several columns, they are not in the ordinary Osgoode Hall news. The account shows that general fraud was charged, that there was an affidavit by Mr. William Laidlaw, K.C., showing not only specific fraud as affecting his clients, hut a general system of fraud in the initiation of the bank. That is what is in the newspapers, and that is what Mr. Boville read. Then it is pointed out in the newspaper accounts that the matter is only tentatively dispos-

ed of, that it will not be actually disposed of until the 1st of November, so that the Department is in a hurry as you see. And then, to make it more easy for the department, to call on Mr. McCarthy, as they do, to withdraw his protest against the issue of the certificate, there are such headlines as: Farmers' Bank avoids threatened windup. Plaintiffs bought out. Oath against oath, and things of this kind. I wondered when I read this letter why the Minister of Finance, having promised to lay this matter before the Treasury Board, was so solicitous to have Mr. McCarthy withdraw this charge. But one is more amazed to find that the very account that is referred to in that letter, and which is the only excuse for writing it, is of a nature to intensify the anxiety of the department to have a thorough and full investigation of this matter. They ask Mr. McCarthy if he still wishes to let the Treasury Board know of the pretty general allegations contained in his letter, and they suggest by their letter that he should not,press it, because of what they had read in the newspapers; and what they read in the newspapers must have been of the character published in the newspapers, and not of a character on which to base a letter of this kind. Mr. McCarthy was not satisfied, he knew that the suit was not settled. What happened was this, and it is set out in the newspapers: Mr. Lindsay got busy, he hied off into the county of Halton, got hold of the clients of Messrs. Laidlaw and McCarthy without the knowledge of these solicitors, bought them off, and came into court with affidavits that these people were settled with, and Mr. Kappelle, representing the plaintiffs' interests in court, objected. There was no' one present representing the general public interest at this proceeding as in the other proceedings in connection with this transaction. The judge said that in as much as it was stated. that the whole matter was settled there was no necessity to proceed further, but he would leave the matter for final decision until November 1. Mr. McCarthy does not altogether agree with the department's view.' He writes back:
Home Life Building, Victoria St.,
Toronto, November 1, 1906.
T. C. Boville, Esq.,
Acting Deputy Minister of Finance, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-With reference to yours of the 31st ultimo, I will be in Ottawa on Monday or Tuesday of next week when I will do myself the pleasure of calling upon yo-u with reference to the subject matter of your letter.
LEIGHTON McCarthy.
This is another circumstance, I submit, to call the attention of the department to the fact that Mr. McCarthy does not regard Mr. LENNOX.
it as so simple a matter that he could write back and say ' Yes.' Then, on November 2, Mr. McCarthy writes in this way. And I call your attention to, the fact, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the complete withdrawal that the department has asked Mr. McCarthy for. It is a qualified withdrawal, as much as to say, ' my clients are now safe, and, so far as they are concerned, I have no further protest to make; but you know what I said, about the other; it is up to you to do what you like.'
Is there anything to show that he saw the minister in the meantime?

Not a syllable. He never did see the minister, so far as we know from anything that has transpired. You see he has it on his mind that he would like to have an interview with the minister; and even after this call-off-your-dog letter from the department, he again says: I would like to go down. Here is the letter to the minister to which I have referred:
Toronto, November 2, 1906. Honourable W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letters of the 8th and 9fh inst.

That is an error. It should be 8th and 19th ult.
-with reference to the application for a certificate made on behalf of the Farmers' Bank, I am advised by those who are instructing me that the claims made by them in the action, brought have been settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties interested in the bank and refunding the money paid by the individuals or returning the notes which had been given. The objections which I made on their behalf to the issue of the certificates are therefore withdrawn. Would yon mind, therefore, returning to me the papers which I forwarded to you?
Mark you, there is this important item of information, not only conveyed by the newspapers to the department, but conveyed personally to the Minister of Finance by this letter of Mr. McCarthy, that the persons interested in the bank had been compelled to take over the subscriptions to relieve these parties who had brought the suit, to buy them off and give them up their notes. The newspapers show, further, that they had been compelled to guarantee them against the double liability to which they otherwise would have been subject. So the matter stood on the third of November, when this letter would arrive.
Now, I want to pause here for a moment that we may see what the situation was at that time and of what circumstances the minister had undoubted knowledge on that day. I submit that in the letter of Mr. McCarthy's withdrawal and by the ac-

counts contained in the newspapers there is a full, a sufficient and complete acknowledgment by the persons interested in promoting the Farmers' Bank, that all the allegations contained in Mr. McCarthy's particulars of claim, as forwarded to the minister, so far as these parties are concerned, were absolutely true. There are some other outstanding features that I shoud refer to as having been before the minister on the third of November. The first is, that, having regard to the fact that this matter was up in court before Travers wrote his letter of the 29th of October, the minister had specific and clear information on the 3rd of November that Travers' letter of the 29th of October, saying that he knew of nothing wrong, was absolutely a.falsehood. That is one item in reference to Travers. The second item is, that the winding up proceedings had been averted by a compromise, and by a surreptitious buying off of the plaintiffs behind the backs of their solicitors effected through Lindsay and Travers, the Travers who afterwards secured the confidence of the minister. Travers was charged in these proceedings, as reported in the Toronto newspapers, to which Mr. Boville refers, with fraud, with gross dishonesty, and with an evasion of the Bank Act, the charge being made by so eminent a K.C. as William Laidlaw, on oath in court. In that statement of fraud others than the plaintiffs-Robert Noble, Dr. Stewart, Major Beattie, and others -were all affected by the frauds; and notwithstanding the settlement of the suit, all the facts as affecting them remained on record on oath at Osgoode Hall, undisposed of, as the minister knew. That a large proportion of the $250,000 was obtained by discount of notes, as the minister, on the 3rd of November, well knew. That moneys actually collected had been wrongfully, and contrary to the Bank Act, unlawfully diverted to the payment of commission and other improper purposes, and charges by the agents and solicitors of the bank, as the minister knew, and that the agents and solicitors of the bank were acting irregularly, dishonestly, and contrary to the Bank Act, as was alleged on oath, as the minister also /'knew. All these circumstances, as I submit, existed on the 3rd of November, to the knowledge of the minister, and were, as I submit, important circumstances to make him hesitate-yes, to make him hesitate even to the extent of refusing-to grant the charter even if nothing more had been shown.
But it does not stop there. I said a few moments ago that the statements that Mr. McCarthy asked to have laid before the Treasury Board were never laid before the Treasury Board. I have proof in the letter of 7th November, 1906, in which Mr. Boville says, addressing Mr. McCarthy:
Referring to your letter of tlie 2nd instant, in the matter of an application of the Farmers' Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence business, I beg to inclose herewith the papers forwarded with your letter of the 19tli October.
Returned on the 7th of November, or some weeks before the application of the Farmers' Bank was made. So we have this point absolutely clear,-these papers were not submitted to the Deputy Minister of Justice, and were not submitted to the Treasury Board. Well, what happened? The funniest thing of all happened. The Deputy Minister, having notified this gemlike character Travers of a difficulty-for he says, ' opposition is offered '-on the 24th of October, is dreadfully afraid he might attempt to explain and create greater difficulty. So having got rid of the evidence of Mr. McCarthy laid before the Minister of Finance, and having refused the repeated offers of Mr. McCarthy to go and discuss the whole matter with the Minister of Finance, on the 7th of November, the verv day on which the papers were returned to Mr. McCarthy, Mr. Boville says the coast is clear-not in those words, but in a more definite form. He does it promptly; he says:
W. R. Travers, Esq.,
General Manager,
The Farmers' Bank of Canada, Toronto, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letter to you of the 2nd inst., inclosing copy of a letter addressed to Mr. Fielding by Mr. Leighton McCarthy by way of a protest to the granting of a certificate to your bank to commence business, I beg to state that I am advised by Mr. McCarthy that the objections which he made to the issue of a certificate have been withdrawn.
That is not true. Mr. McCarthy had made a series of objections on behalf of his clients, and so far as his clients were concerned, those charges were withdrawn because these people had been bought off. But what I point out is this: Why in the name of common sense, why in the name of the rights of the people, has the Department of Finance to go out of its way to say:	Don't answer that letter, don't take
any chances, or complicate matters? We have got rid of the McCarthy letter, don't say anything. It is like Alphonse and Gaston. ' Don't commit yourself, my dear Alphonse,' says the Minister of Finance. ' I certainly will not, my dear Gaston,' replies innocent Mr. Travers. Well, that brings the record down to the application. The application was forwarded on the 27th of November, inclosed in a letter from Mr. Travers. It reached here on the 28th of November. We begin to do something then, there is no delay after that. On the 29th Mr. Travers is

here, and these papers are here before him. There is his application, there is his affidavit and his declaration verifying it. I need only read two clauses of that declaration, the fourth and the fifth, and these are the two clauses upon which the Department of Finance rely when they are trying to satisfy the Bankers' Association later on:
4.	On the 23rd day of October, 1906 (says Travers in his declaration), there had been actually bona fide subscribed 5,757 shares of the capital stock of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, and I have had personal knowledge of the applications and subscriptions, and each and all of the said subscriptions is and are on the printed form of application-a copy of which is now produced and marked Exhibit C to this my declaration, and that the said subscriptions appeared on the stock books of the said bank, and that a sum beyond $250,000 thereof in cash has been actually paid in by the subscribers of the same.
5.	Now shown to me and marked Exhibit D to this my declaration is a list of the subscribers to the capital stock of the said bank correctely setting forth as to each subscription the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of shares subscribed for by him, the amount of such shares and the amount paid in thereon. Each of the said subscriptions is a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the said bank.
That is the statement made on oath by Mr. Travers, and filed with the department. It will be admitted surely that if, to the knowledge of the minister, that declaration was in any substantial matter untrue, it stamped Mr. Travers in such a way that his testimony ought not to be received. What will vou say, Mr. Speaker, when I tell you that in that very application, attached to it as exhibit D referred to in the clauses I have just read, in that very list of subscribers are the names of the men who were plaintiffs in that 'suit, and whose names, it was admitted on oath, were every one of them obtained by fraud ? Let me read the names :
John McLeod, Milton, Out., 1 share, $100, $50 paid; John Sproat, Mansewood, Ont., 100 shares, $10,000, $1,000 paid; Geo. Gastle, Milton, Ont., 10 shares, $1,000, $1,000 paid; Ein-lay McCallum, Milton. Ont., 10 shares, $1,000. $1,000 paid; W. A. Dixon, Milton, Ont., 50 shares, $5,000,	$500 paid; James Murray,
of subscribers, are the names of the men Mansewood, Ont., 10 shares, $1,000, $300 paid; John Stewart, Milton, Out., 10 shares $1,000, $100 paid; Geo. Denoon, Milton, Ont., 20 shares, $2,000, $2,000 paid; Robert Hume, Milton, Ont., 10 shares, $1,000, $100 paid; William McLean, Milton, Ont., 5 shares, $500, $50 paid: Wm. Harris, Milton, Ont., 5 shares, $500, $500 paid.
Yet there had been a suit of which the Minister of Finance and his Deputy Minister had complete knowledge, all of record in their own office, and brought to their knowledge by the newspapers, showing that | as regards those eleven names, there was Mr. LENNOX.
enacted an organized system of fraud. There had been a refund, and these parties had been guaranteed and had been bought off, as the ' Globe ' and ' Mail ' and other Toronto newspapers, alleged. Yet their names are here as bona fide subscribers. They had given promissory notes, and the money had been refunded, and they had been bought up and silenced, and the fraud was compromised, the felony was compounded by those parties who subsequently came to the Minister of Finance to get this certificate. The next step I need not spend any time upon. The minister forwards a file of the papers to the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the Deputy Minister of Justice says:
As regards the statements of Wm. R. Travers, they are sufficient if they are accepted.
And he leaves it in that way. But even if the Deputy Minister of Justice has made a mistake in this matter, he was not much to blame, because he was not furnished with material upon which to found a judgment upon the merits. I am glad that it is not pretended that the minister submitted anything more to the Deputy Minister of Justice than the mere question as to whether the form of the document as a legal document was sufficient for the purpose. Now wre began to have things done promptly again after a considerable lack of promptness. Mr. Travers' application came on the 28th of November ; Mr. Travers was here on the 29th November. On the 30th of November we have a letter from Mr. Fielding to Mr. Travers. After referring to his inability to see Mr. Travers the day before, the minister says:
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to ns that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actanlly an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which had reached ns in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to ns. I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers' Bank, but that the amount set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
Alphonse and Gaston come in again. Why did not the Finance Minister talk to this man in a business way? If a man goes into a bank, and they find that he has been guilty of misrepresentation and fraud, and he applies for a loan, the bank manager meets him and says; ' I want this matter

cleared up before you can do any business with us; if you show that you are an honest man, we will deal with you; if you cannot show that, you will not have any business dealings with us.5 The Minister of Finance, however, was very polite and inoffensive to Mr. Travers in referring _ to what had been done in some other case, imaginary or real, as much as to say: 'You must not imagine for a moment that we think there was anything wrong in your case, but because there was something wrong in another case, we want to be exceedingly careful, and I shall be glad to have an assurance from you that all is right." What did the Minister of Finance mean by 'an insurance5 in that case? Mr. Travers had made a solemn declaration which in law has all the force and effect of an oath rendering him liable to the penalties of perjury. When the minister dictated that letter, did he mean anything or was it a sham? I will not for one moment believe that he meant a sham; no one knows the Minister of Finance would be mean enough to suggest that. He meant what he said-he meant:	'I want some assurance; I want
something better than your declaration; I want some proof that this matter is square and bona fide. I have your declaration; I have your letter of the 29th of October; I know that that letter was false; I have your declaration of the 27th of November; I know that it bears on its face the absolute refutation of its truth; and_I want some assurance.5 And what happens? The minister meant well; no doubt he did. But smooth Mr. Travers came to the minister, and the minister cross-examined him, he says; and what was the result? The result was nothing. After having determined to have an assurance, which meant some other evidence beyond the evidence of a man whom the records had convicted as being unreliable, he had an interview with that man, and, whether by the persuasion of Mr. Travers or by the persuasion of Mr. Calvert, perhaps the guarantee of Mr. Calvert that Mr. Travers was a superior class of man, and, therefore, eminently reliable, notwithstanding the fact that he had sent a false letter, notwithstanding the fact that he had made a false declaration which was on file in the department at that time, in some way which I cannot understand, which I am not bound to explain, the Minister of Finance decided to let this matter go through-a matter which I believe will be one of continued regret to the House, and the country, and, I have no doubt, to do the minister justice, a matter of regret to him also. Therefore, what we find is this, that instead of having any assurance from Mr. Travers, we have_ merely his verbal statement to the Minister of Finance, followed by this letter merely for the purpose of record:
Ottawa, November 30, 1906.

Fielding,
In reply to your letter of the 30th of November, I have to say that in the case of the Farmers5 Bank of Canada the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way mentioned by you.
What does that mean? It certainly does not meet the letter which the Minister of Finance wrote; and if the cross-examination was no more successful than was the letter elicited afterwards, the tender conscience of Mr. Travers was not very much hurt. The Minister of Finance, when he wrote the letter of the 30th of November, meant what he said. He realized that with the evidences of dishonesty which were spread out upon the record in his own office, he could not and dare not accept the statement of Mr. Travers, and he writes to him for further assurance; but, by some means, I know not what-some means which are very much to be regretted -honest, so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, I have no doubt at all, but by some unfortunate circumstance, the matter was allowed to go through, notwithstanding the determination of the minister a few hours before that it could not go through without further evidence. That is the most charitable construction I can put upon it. Now, on the same 30th of November, the order in council was made; on the same 30th of November the certificate of the order in council was issued; on the- same 30th of November the certificate was transmitted to Mr. Travers, addressed to Toronto, but handed to him here;' on the same 30th of November the balance of the deposit, $245,000, was handed over to Mr. Travers; pretty prompt action, with this fortunate circumstance, that if it had been availed of, the Minister of Finance could have prevented the payment of that cheque if he had thought fit to do so. What have we on the 30th of November? We have the letter of the Minister of Finance to Mr. Travers; we have the interview of Mr. Travers with the Minister of Finance; we have the letter of Mr. Travers to the Minister of Finance; we have the order in council made upon the matter-all being carefully submitted to the Treasury Board;_we have the certificate issued by the officials of the department; we have the cheque handed over, and the certificate handed over, and the whole matter closed-seven distinct transactions all in one busy day, the 30th of November, when it is urgent that this matter should be closed. This pretty nearly ends the chapter of incidents. We have also on that day the receipt for the cheque from Mr. Travers. On the 30th of November-dated the same day, and possibly here the same day; it could not have reached the Minister of Finance or else he would not do as he did-we have a letter

of the 30th November [DOT]written by Mr. E. S. Clouston, president of the Canadian Bankers Association, an institution acting under the Bank Act, a branch, so to speak, of the administration of public affairs in Canada; we have a letter from him showing that the representations of Mr. Travers were false. I read that letter:

Montreal, November 30, 1906.
*Farmers' Bank of Canada.
T. C. Boville, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
.,Pear, In connection with the application of the Farmers' Bank of Canada for the usual certificate from the Treasury Board, I have reason to believe that the money lodged, or to be lodged, at Ottawa as stock subecrip-anAStwnn0ti be regarded as paid-up capital, ? 1f,rge Proportion of the amount necessary to the obtaining of a certificate is a loan made upon the promise of its payment when returned by your department.
Permit me to request that, if only for the protection of the public, the Treasury Board will exercise its right to refuse to issue a certificate if it thinks best so to do, until a thorough investigation has been made into the circumstances stated herein.

President.
And I may state to you, Mr. Speaker, so as to have it on record, that this statement turns out to be absolutely true-at least $20,000 was. borrowed, independently of the amounts that were borrowed on promissory notes, to make up the deposit with the government. Now, Sir, -what should the Finance Minister have done? I say in the	first	place that	he shouldhave refused	the	certificate	and	thatit never should have been issued. The next point I have to make is that even though through improvidence or mistake this certificate was issued in good faith, it was still the duty of the Minister of Finance to see that the result should not be prejudicial to	the	public. I	will	notquibble as to the question of cancellation, I will not argue as to the question of a royal commission.	Notwithstanding	the
fact that a royal commission did issue in the insurance case on less grounds than existed here and without consulting parliament-, and under the same Act that would have to be invoked in this case, I do not need to argue upon that point. I say that when on 'the 30th November or the 1st December at latest, the knowledge came to the Finance Minister that he had been deceived, it became the duty of the minister, beyond question, to see that the public should not be defrauded. Can there be any doubt about it? The cheque was not paid; Mr. Travers was a needy man, Mr. Travers was a criminal, the 1 Mr. LENNOX.
Minister of Finance knew it on the 1st December if he did not know it before, and a criminal is a coward the world over, and the minister had only to telegraph Mr. Travers to come to Ottawa, and he would have come by the first train. And criminal as he was to the knowledge of the minister on the 1st December if not before, the minister had him at his feet, and could have shaken him as a mastiff shakes a terrier, and he could have made him disgorge that cheque in less time than I take to tell you, -and he could have made him give up that certificate rather -than be landed behind the bars. That was the duty of the minister. I was going to call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the peculiar promptness with which everything that facilitated the action of Mr. Travers transpired. I do not want to insinuate for a moment-and I want it to be distinctly understood that in What I say this afternoon I do not make any charge of want of good faith against the minister-but it is a circumstance unfortunate in itself that this fatal rapidity occurred in this particular case when there was every reason fo-r delay, and investigation. There ought to have been such an investigation as would inevitably have prevented the happening of this disaster which will ruin a large number of people in the province of Ontario. Therefore, without imputing to the Minister of Finance any wilful wrong or misconduct or want of good faith, I do think that the Minister of Finance, as a public man in his public capacity, does deserve the censure of this House and of the people of Canada through this House, for the great wrong that has been inflicted upon a large number of deserving people throughout title province of Ontario; many of whom cannot afford the enormous loss entailed upon them. I say so because the minister was warned time and again. The minister is a clever man, we all recognize that- sometimes we think he ought to put it to better account-but he is a clever, astute man, and a warning to such a man ought to have had some effect. He was warned by his own opinion about the matter; he was warned when these men came back a second time for the renewal of their charter, because, as he tells us himself, he realized that having hawked their stock about for two years unsuccessfully, they were not the best class of men to go into the banking business. That should have made him more cautious about investigating before granting the certificate. He was warned by previous cases -as to which he writes to Mr. Travers; he was warned by Travers' letter of the 29th October, which from his own knowledge of the circumstances was false; he was -warned many times by the hon. member for Halton-and when I say that I do not choose to believe the member for

Halton in preference to the Minister of Finance except upon the broad principle that having faith in both of them as being anxious to tell what is right, I recognize that the member for Halton has fewer charges upon his memory than has the Minister of Finance and also that he is speaking of a fact positive, and the Minister of Finance is only speaking of a matter of recollection. I will say nothing about the warning of Mr. Osier, M.P. for Toronto, because that is in dispute. He was warned by Mr. McCarthy's letters of the 8th and 19th October, and he refused the offers that Mr. McCarthy made to have a personal interview. He was warned by the legal documents explicit, full and direct as to general misconduct, evasion of the Bank Act, and dishonesty, as disclosed in the legal documents forwarded by Mr. McCarthy. He was warned by the newspapers which contained a full account of the fraud by which these Halton farmers had been rohbed, and he was warned by the qualified and cautious withdrawal of Mr. McCarthy which was as much as to say: You do as you like, but I want to have it understood that I only withdraw so far as my clients are concerned. And, the Minister of Finance was warned, in a way that I cannot understand his ignoring, by the conclusive falsehoods stamped upon the face of the declaration and application which Mr. Travers filed in his department
This being the case, reluctant as I am to men on both sides. Had the shareholders
not met and constituted a board of direcsay anything in anv degree harsh as regards the Minister of Finance, having great regard for him as a public man, yet realiz-inz as I do that he failed to discharge the duty which he owed parliament in connection with the Farmers' Bank, I beg to move:
That all the words after the word ' that ' in the proposed motion he omitted and the following substituted therefor:-
This House regrets that in permitting the Farmers' Bank of Canada to commence and to continue business, the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board failed to exercise such proper care and to take such reasonable precautions as were necessary to prevent evasion of the law and to protect the public interest.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one passage in the speech of the hon. gentleman's in which I can most heartily agree. It is that in which he said it is deeply to be regretted that the Farmers' Bank was allowed to he organized. Most heartily do I concur in that regret. The occasion is one of these, however, in which it is so much easier to be wise in a later stage than at the beginning. Looking at the matter to-day in the light of recent events, in the light, of the failure of the bank, in the light of all the facts that are now known, one naturally comes to the
conclusion that the whole transaction was-most regrettable. It is, however, very difficult to-day to bring a fair judgment to bear upon an event which was not judged in the light of to-day, but which had to be judged in the light of things as they stood some four years ago.
We had a very full discussion of this subject a short time ago, and so far as I can see my hon. friend has not brought forward any point which was not fully gone into in that discussion. At all events I cannot undertake to add anything to the information before the House, and therefore I do not intend to occupy the attention of the House except very briefly. The granting of this certificate to the hank was no doubt a matter of importance, but I do not think it had exactly the importance which my hon. friend seems to attach to it. But for the granting of the certificate, he said, this bank would not have been organized. That is true, but the same thing may be said regarding many other stages in the Bank's affairs.	1 ^a' I '
farmers not subscribed for stock, the hank would not have been organized. Had application not been made for a charter, it would not have been organized. Had the charter not been approved by the Committee on Banking and Commerce, it could not have been organized. Nor would it ^ave been organized had the charter not been approved in this House by hon. gentletors, and had the board of directors not taken all the initial steps required by the Bank Act, the organization of the bank could not have been completed. If any one of these steps had not been taken the bank certainly would not have been organized, because it required each and every one of them to give it a legal standing.
There are several stages in the organizing of a bank, the first of which is the granting of a charter. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has alluded to that as if the_ government, and the Minister of Finance in particular were speciallv responsible for the granting of this charter. On reflection, I think he will admit that that is not a fair argument at all. There is a parliamentary sense in which the government have to do with all legislation, but we know that as a matter of fact, in the management of private Bills, the government do not usually interfere. For instance there was a Bill last session in regard to which a number of members of the government happened to unite in its support, and we were told that we were interfering with the privileges of members, and that the government should not interfere in a private Bill. So that the idea that the government had anything in particular to do with the granting of the charter to this bank is an entire-

ly mistaken one. I was a member of the Banking and Commerce Committee. I do not recollect whether my hon. friend was or not.
I was not. I may say to the hon. minister that I did not address myself at all to the incorporation of the bank, and I agree in all "he has said in that connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend repeatedly referred to the granting of the charter. He did not dwell on it, I admit, but he said sufficient to imply that in the granting of this charter in the beginning some wrong was done. As a matter of fact that Bill came before the Banking and Commerce Committee like any other private Bill. A charter was granted, then an extension was given, and later on another extension. I was in this position. Mv hon. friend has represented that for some mysterious reason I was particularly anxious and zealous in having this bank organized, and give Mr. Travers a chance to go into business. Well, those who know anything about the course I took in the Banking and Commerce Committee know that my position was the very reverse. I do not remember the first extension, but I know that I was decidedly unfriendly to the- second.- I was not unfriendly because I thought there was anything wrong or suspected anything crooked, but simply because I regretted to find a number of farmers undertaking to organize a bank. I was afraid that there were going into a business for which they were not well fitted, and that it might not be a success. I had, however, no reason to suspect anything wrong. When, therefore, the second extension was asked I opposed it. The committee, however, consented to give the six months extension, and that was not the fault of the government or the opposition. I could not say what particular view any member on either side took on that occasion, but I do remember my own, and I know that the committee came to the conclusion that a six months extension should be given. All the members of the committee who gave them that extension are equally responsible with those on this side of the House. When the measure came to the House I do not remember anything particular about it. It travelled the usual course of a private Bill, and all members of the House, irrespective of party who allowed that private Bill to become law, are -equally responsible for the granting of the -charter.
Now, we come to the question of the certificate. My hon. friend has dwelt upon the letters of Mr. McCarthy. What the record shows is that Mr. McCarthy wrote a letter filing objections to the granting of the certificate, aind he was informed that application for the granting of the Mr. FIELDING
certificate had not yet been received, but that when the application for the granting of the certificate should come in then his representation would receive consideration and the papers *would be submitted to the Treasury Board. The -application did come in, but Mr. McCarthy wrote a letter, which is on the record and which my hon. friend read, withdrawing the statements he had made. It is not an unusual thing in the organization of a company to find some shareholders who become discontented and wish to withdraw. Mr. McCarthy, representing -some of the -shareholders, filed a protest; a little later he withdrew the protest, and asked that the papers be sent back to him. That is the whole story of that matter. My hon. friend said that Mr. McCarthy was very anxious to come to Ottawa and discuss the matter, but we would not let him. The hon. gentleman knows enough of M>r. McCarthy to know that if he wanted to come to Ottawa to see a minister, whether of the present cabinet or any other, Mr. McCarthy would come and see that minister. As a matter of fact, while intimating his willingness to come when necessary, Mr. McCarthy, so far as my recollection goes, did hot come to Ottawa. Later on, Mr. McCarthy having withdrawn his objection, proceedings went on towards the granting of the certificate. On a certain date, November 30, the certificate was granted. My -hon. friend-thinks there was a remarkable and undue haste in the events of that day. Now, once it was decided, whether wisely or unwisely may be a matter of debate, that that -certificate should be granted, it would become a mere matter of procedure in the department, and I am certainly far from complaining of my deputy for expediting it. I am of the opinion that once a decision on any point is reached, it is the duty of the officials to carry out that decision as promptly as possible, and if in that instance the deputy minister expedited the transaction I should not see in it anything to suspect; I should, on the contrary, be disposed to commend that official for having -carried out as promptly as possible a matter which had been decided by the proper authorities. My hon. friend tried to read into M-r. Boville's letters something mysterious; he implied that Mr. Boville was trying to prevent Mr. McCarthy from coming here. I do not complain of my hon. friend- suggesting all sorts of faults on the part of the minister-although he was very kind in his personal references to myself-for after all that is in the game of public affairs;
I do think, however, he should not be ungenerous enough to suggest, or imply, -that the deputy minister, who is not responsible, I am responsible, in the writing of

these letters, whether as to the dates or to the terms, had any other purpose than to do his duty as a public official.
In whatever I said with reference to Mr. Boville, I regarded him as identical with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am responsible.
Mr. LENNOX-and therefore the minister becomes responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that while a minister is responsible, matters of this sort have very largely to be carried out by his officials. That does not relieve him of responsibility, I am responsible, all through; but my hon. friend will see that if there was a conspiracy in this matter not only must I have been a conspirator, but Mr. Boville must have been one also. I shall not quarrel with him if he puts me in that light, but I want him to spare Mr. Boville who is a good official and merely wanted to do his duty.
It has been said that certain allegations were made against the organization of the bank and that they were withdrawn. Then, we have filed an affidavit of Travers and the next day, after we had agreed to grant the certificate, we received a letter from Sir Edward Clouston, President of the Bankers' Association. It has been clearly shown that that letter .reached us after the decision-had -been reached; after the certificate had been delivered to Travers, or at all events had been issued, and I presume it was delivered to Travers. All that that letter contained was a statement of Sir Edward that he had reason to believe that notes were given. Against that we have the affidavit, the sworn statement of Mr. Travers, and Mr. Travers at that time was a reputable man. I want the House to take note of that carefully; it is of the utmost importance. Even if it had been an open question, which it was not, as the certificate had been given and the question was closed, we had then on the one side, the statement of Sir Edward that he had reason to believe that notes were given, and on the other side the sworn affidavit of Travers that the matter was in proper shape, that the money had been paid in cash, and that the conditions of the Bank Act had been complied with. It is easy to-day to treat Travers as a criminal and to say his testimony was worth nothing, but when Travers made that affidavit he was a man of good standing and good repute in the eyes of the world and we had no right to regard him as otherwise. My hon. friend has stated that Travers was at that time a criminal, that he was known to be a criminal, that it had been shown by the public papers
in the city of Toronto that Travers was at that time a criminal. We all know in the light of later events that Travers has been convicted and sent to the penitentiary, but it is not correct to say that at that time he was a criminal; he was a man in good standing. We were bound to treat him as such, bound to pay respect to his affidavit, just as we would to the affidavit of any man of Tepute.
Were there not eleven names on the affidavit that had been withdrawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot from memory deal with that particular aspect of the question. But there remained the fact that he had given his sworn affidavit that the money was up in cash. That was the essential feature of the whole thing, and his affidavit at that time was just as good as the statement or affidavit of any one else, better than the mere statement of any other gentleman, no matter how eminent, who merely said he had reason to believe. I think'it is of the utmost importance in judging of this matter to bear in mind the fact that Travers was at that time a man of good repute. It is the_ essence of the whole question. As I said, it is difficult now, when Travers is a convicted criminal, to see the transaction in the proper light. My hon. friend says that Travers is not only a criminal now, but was a criminal then, ~ and was-known- to be so from the published statements in the Toronto papers.

The minister said in his former speech that he had no knowledge at all of Travers. Had the minister taken any step3 to ascertain, from persons who could give him information, Mr. Travers' standing, financial and otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I made no such special inquiry. I want to show that my view of Travers' good standing must have been the view which prevailed among a good many other men, possibly better qualified than I to judge of it. Travers organized his bank in the city of Toronto. Travers obtained the co-operation of well known, reputable citizens. Mr. Travers was associated with these gentlemen who joined him in the responsibility of the bank. Is it conceivable that, if he was a criminal, these gentlemen of repute in the province of Ontario would have associated themselves with him and made him manager of the bank? Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) think that conceivable? I will give him a further point. Mr. Travers, down to the day of the failure of the bank, was regarded by the government of Ontario as a reputable man, for they entrusted him ' with a considerable sum of the public

funds of the province of Ontario. If the government of Ontario, down to a few months ago, at the very time when the bank failed, regarded him as a man of repute, surely, I could not be regarded as mistaken when he came to me if, in the absence of anything to the contrary, I treated him as a man of repute.
May I be permitted a question? How did the government of Ontario entrust Mr. Travers with their money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I see it stated in a public return of liabilities that the province of Ontario had $25,000 in the Farmers' Bank. That is all I know about it.

Deposited in one of the
branches?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That makes no difference; it was entrusted to the bank of which Mr. Travers was^ manager, and if he were known as a criminal-not only now, but at that time-is it conceivable that the government of Ontario would have deposited $25,000 in the bank of which he was manager? I am not finding fault with the government of Ontario. I am supposing that what they did, was done, as they believed it, in the public interest. I have no purpose in referring to it except to show that in all these transactions we must regard Mr. Travers as, at that time, a man of repute.
Now, the irregularity of the proceedings was in regard to the taking of notes. I do not wish to minimize that. I quite say that if we had known at that time what we learned later we would have refused the certificate. But there is a misunderstanding abroad as to the results of that. It should be understood that, as I am informed-speaking of what is recorded in the press-nearly all these notes were paid. If there was irregularity at the time the certificate was obtained the notes were paid; the bank had the capital; no man in the province of Ontario has suffered a loss, so far as I know, of a single dollar by reason of the fact that notes were signed instead of putting up cash. The notes were converted, as I understand it, into cash. If that is not the case, I shall be glad to be corrected.

I understand the minister to say that he was not aware that they were paying their subscribed stock by notes. But did not Mr. McCarthy draw attention to that fact when he stated, in speaking of his clients, that they had been handed back their notes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. McCarthy had filed objections, but those objections were withdrawn.

But he made the statement of which I speak.
Mr. FIELDING

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He objected to the is-sue_ of the certificate. Later he said:	I
desire to withdraw my objection; send me back the papers. And the papers were sent back. I merely want to put the case as it stood
But there was a clear statement in Mr. McCarthy's letter that notes had been signed..

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But, against that, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will see that that apparently was settled. The form in which the matter stood at all events, "was that Mr. McCarthy withdrew his objections. And later we have the statement of Mr. Travers on oath that he had his money put up in cash. That was the evidence on which we issued the certificate. Say, if you like, that it was insufficient. In looking back on it now I may say that had I known more I would have looked into the matter more carefully. We can all be wise in the later years. But at that time we had every reason to believe that Mr. Travers was acting in good faith and

Does not the minister know that the statement on which he says he relied was disputed ? It was stated by Travers that Mr. McCarthy had alleged the opposite. True, Mr. McCarthy withdrew his formal objections, but that, surely, did not remove from the minister's mind the knowledge of the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood that Mr. McCarthy's withdrawing put that matter out of the question. Whether it was wise or unwise that is the way it struck me. Eeference has been made once or twice to a former member of this House, Mr. Calvert. I wish to say that any hon. gentleman who associates the name of Mr. Calvert with the issue of that certificate does Mr. Calvert an injustice. So little effect did it have on my mind that until I was reminded of it, I did not remember that Mr. Calvert had introduced Mr. Travers to me. But Mr. Calvert, in his conversation, never exchanged a word with respect to the issue of the certificate. He confined himself to the introduction of Mr. Travers-and even the introduction was not necessary, because, of course, no man needs an introduction to a minister when he comes to Ottawa on public business. But 1 think it only fair to say that I am not conscious that Mr. Calvert ever spoke a word to me concerning the issue of the certificate. So, whatever else is said it is not fair to blame that gentleman, who .is not now in parliament, but holds an important public position. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) wishes to convey the impression-I do not say unfairly, because the spirit of his remarks was very fair-that

throughout this transaction there was a desire on the part of the Finance Department to expedite the matter of issuing the certificate. That was the very opposite to my own mind in the matter. If I erred in this matter, I erred from the fact that I feared that I was perhaps going to do injustice to the farmers who wanted the certificate. I did regret at an early stage that they were going into the business. I should have rejoiced could I have found satisfactory reasons to refuse this certificate. But I found that we had precisely the same evidence before us as had been before us in other cases. And I asked myself:	What right have I to say that the
farmers shall be refused a certificate when, they come to us with the same information and the same evidence as had been furnished in other cases? Cases could be shown, one at all events, in which a certificate was granted without an affidavit at all; I do not say wrongly granted, I am sure it was done in good faith. We have to be governed largely by precedent in these things. If we had refused that certificate and if, in consequence, the bank had been wound up, involving a veTy serious loss to shareholders who 'had put their money into it and had incurred the expense of organization, I know what would have followed. These good farmers would have turned round and said:	Mr. Fielding -was ready
enoirgh to grant certificates to other banks, but this was a farmers' bank, we were small men, poor people.; -we-wanted a charter, and we complied with the law and did everything that others had been required to do, yet v/e were refused. I ask hen. gentlemen opposite, would not that have been the position? I do not pretend to say, looking over this matter, that there is nothing to regret. I do deeply regret it. All I ask is that the gentlemen who consider this subject 'will endeavour to look at it, not in the light of to-day, but in the iight of events as they existed at that time, four and a-half years ago. I ask them to remember the standing of Mr. Travers, to remember that he placed before me all the evidence which any other applicant for a bank certificate usually gave. If the matter is looked at in that light, I think it will be seen that there is no real cause to complain of what was done.

I do not intend to say more than a few words on the subject, as the matter was so thoroughly discussed on a former occasion and lias been so well covered to-day by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). I think the matter comes down to a question of whether the facts known at the time justified the issue cf a certificate. Nor do I wish to find fault with the minister on
account of his intentions; I think his in tentions were good.
We have the question whether or not the Minister of Finance, aedng as the trustee of the people of Canada, exercised the ordinary and usual precaution that a trustee under similar circumstances would exercise, and if he did that, I am prepared to say he has discharged his duties in that regard. In forming a conclusion as (to [DOT] whether he did exercise proper care, we have to find out what was in his mind at the time, because a man is only guilty of an offence according to the knowledge he has in his mind at the time. The Finance. Minister admits that he opposed the incorporation of the bank, and he did that because he thought that to incorporate a Farmers' Bank, a bank of that name might lead unsuspecting farmers to banking trans-* actions with which they were unfamiliar.
He was opposed to that idea, and when the charter came to be renewed the second time, he would not grant an extension further than six months. I want to point out that the Act granting the extension for six months was passed on the 26th of June, in the year in which the certificate was granted. So that would be prominently in the mind of the Minister of Finance five months afterwards when he granted the certificate. The first point I want to touch upon as giving the minister some evidence of the transactions which were going on in connection with the organization of this
bank, is the statement made bv the hon_________
member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). I am of course arguing on a question of memory between the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Halton. The Minister of Finance says that be has a distinct recollection that nothing was said to him by the member for Halton as to this bank having received some notes in part payment of subscriptions, and that these notes were being discounted for the purposfe of raising money to be deposited with the Receiver General. In the first place, I would think that as the Minister of Finanefe i3 a very busy man, and as this was a matter which particularly interested the member for Halton, a matter particularly within his own knowledge and affecting his constituents, the presumption is in favour of the memory of the hon. member for Halton as being correct. The member for Halton says himself that he had seen the notes in question which had been given in part payment for subscriptions, he had seen these in the hands of the solicitor, when he says he spoke to the Minister of Finance about if. The Minister of Finance on the other hand says that the member for Halton never spoke to him with reference to it. He admits there were certain conversations between the member for Halton and himself, and that these

conversations were confined exclusively to the question of the charter or tire organization of the bank. They were, therefore, according to the memory of the minister, confined to that aspect of the case and to what took place in the Banking and Commerce Committee, I presume, where the matter was discussed. Now, if that is the case, how could we consider that to be a private matter? The minister complains of the member for Halton for divulging a private matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not complain. I said I had no fault to find with the member for Halton.
I am merely speaking as to the minister's recollection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not complain of the member for Halton for divulging a private matter, I made no complaint against him on that point.
Nevertheless the Finance Minister says that the conversations were of such a character as would justify him in characterizing them as private conversations. Is that not right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except as that would imply any reflection on the member for Halton in repeating them.

My point is that as a matter of recollection, if the conversation between the member for Halton and the Minister of Finance were confined exclusively to what took place in the Banking and Commerce Committee regarding the organization of this bank, that would not be private conversation; therefore when he says that what took place he regarded as private conversation corroborates the belief that what was in the mind of the Minister of Finance was something else, and was not the question of organization of this hank when it was discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that arose out of my opposition in the Banking and Commerce Committee.

I think that very fact alone shows that what the member for Halton told the Minister of Finance was something that did not take place in the Banking and Commerce Committee, but was something which the minister might think was of a private nature. The member for Halton says that it was a fact that he had seen the notes given in part payment for subscription of stock in this bank, and that he went to the Minister of Finance and told him this, that he was troubled about the matter, and wished the minister to take some action with regard to it That is the way the matter stands be-Mr. MIDDLEBRO
tween the Minister of Finance and the member for Halton.
Well, that is the second item of which the Minister of Finance should have taken note. Now I come to the third. A member cf this House in whom no doubt the Minister of Finance has absolute confidence, that is, Mr. McCarthy, writes to the Minister of Finance on the 8th of October, and he says to the minister:	I am acting for
a number of people who are alleged to have subscribed for stock in the Farmers' Bank, and I say their stock has been obtained from them by fraud, I say that notes have been taken from these clients of mine by fraud in payment of their stock, and I want * you to do nothing until this matter is thoroughly investigated. Then Mr. McCarthy follows that up by another letter, and this makes the strong point in the whole case against the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has admitted to me in answer to a question I put to him in the House when he v'as making his statement:

In view of the letter written by Mr. McCarthy on the 19th of October, in which he stated that he had brought action on behalf of certain persons, and of the persons who were subscribers to the funds of the bank, does not the minister consider that that was sufficient warrant, notwithstanding the faot that Mr. McCarthy on their behalf subsequently withdrew his objection, for believing that there was irregularity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we had had no later information, I think my hon. friend's criticism would be just, but after that we did receive the solemn declaration of Travers.
Now let us see' what the further letter from Mr. McCarthy says, bearing in mind what the Finance Minister has admitted, that he thought the first letter would have justified him in refusing the certificate. The first letter says there has been fraud of the various kinds mentioned in the letter, and of the various kinds mentioned in the writ, that men had been put on there as directors who were not diiectors, that they had taken notes instead of cash, and they v. ere discounting those notes and putting the proceeds of those notes into the Department of the Receiver General Now the minister says that if that were true he would be justified in withholding the certificate. Mr. McCarthy writes back and 'says:
I am advised by those who are instructing me that the claims made by them in the action _ brought have been settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties interested in the bank, and refunding the money paid by the individuals, or returning the notes which had been given.
So in what the minister characterizes as a withdrawal by Mr. McCarthy, there is

the positive assertion by him that notes were given in payment of stock, and that is illegal according to law. Now, I would iike to ask the Finance Minister by what process of reasoning can he characterize that as a withdrawal which places on record the fact that there was an infringement of the Act? I would characterize that as nothing more or less than a confirmation of what had been alleged in the former letter; and I , say further, that when Mr. McCarthy made this accusation that certain things had been done, and when the government was told of the return of these securities and notes, it was the most complete proof that the parties had been guilty of the charges Mr. McCarthy had laid against them. Under these circumstances, I do not see how the Minister of Finance could possibly have granted this certificate. Upon that evidence alone the Minister of Finance or his department or his officials did not exercise that ordinary reasonable care and diligence which we expect from ordinary men; but, when they are acting in a judiciary or public character we have a right to exoect from them a much greater degree of care and diligence. The courts of this country, upon the question being put to them on that evidence alone, whether the Minister of Finance had exercised that ordinary care and prudence which should be exercised by a trustee would say that he had not, and he would be liable as a trustee or executor for the consequences of that act. But we have more than that. We have the evidence that the Deputy Minister knew, according to a report in a Toronto newspaper, of what had taken place in the court at Toronto; we have the evidence of Mr. Laidlaw, an eminent K. C. of Toronto, who swears in an affidavit that the endorsements sent by Mr. McCarthy were true. That affidavit has been ignored for the affidavit of Mr. Travers; the statements of Mr. McCarthy have been ignored for the statements of Mr. Travers; the judgment of the court in Toronto has been ignored for the statements of Mr. Travers; and the recollection of my hon. friend from Halton has been ignored for the statements of Mr. Travers. All these matters which had come to the Minister of Finance have been ignored in favour of Mr Travers. I would like to ask the minister this question:	Was he putting a hypothetical case
to Mr. Travers when he said to him: ' It has come to our knowledge that in some cases notes have been given instead of cash for payments of subscriptions'; or was he putting an actual case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend. I had heard gossip in banking circles regarding the organization of a previous bank. I had no information beyond the whispers that went around among
banking men as to the manner in which a certain bank had been organized.

I do not know that
I would be justified in asking the minister the name of the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not care to give that.
It seems to me that it makes it all the harder for the Finance Minister to get away from blame in the present case if he had another instance within his own knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not say I had any knowledge of it. I had heard gossip of that kind in banking circles

The minister had heard gossip that another bank had either attempted to do or had done what this bank did. If it had attempted to do the same thing, he must have headed it off, and made it comply with the law.
